To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intracortrical GM and subjacent white-matter T1-weighted MRI signal intensity is a sensitive marker of neurodevelopment and age-related cortical changes, which are not captured by cortical thickness.
the thickness and T1 signal intensity of the cerebral cortex are sensitive to different maturational and age-related processes, which can be distinguished using a novel surface mapping method.
cortical thickness and intracortical signal intensity are sensitive measures for different cortical maturations and aging-related processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the cerebral cortex.
the question of how the human cerebral cortex develops and ages and how this can be quantitatively described.
the neurobiological processes of brain development and aging and how they relate to the structure and function of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thickness of the cortex decreases with age in a monotone fashion and this is not a reflection of the neurobiology that underlies this change.

the T1 signal of gray matter is a better indicator of neurodevelopment than cortical thickness, whereas cortical thickness is a better indicator than the T1 signal for age-related changes in cortical structure.
cortical thickness is more sensitive to the effects of cortical atrophy in aging, and intracortical T1 signal intensity is more sensitive to cortical development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of cortical thickness and T2* or R2* signal intensity can be used to distinguish maturational from aging-related changes.
the cortical thickness and T2* signal intensity are both sensitive to different cortical aging and development-related processes.
cortical maturation and aging are characterized by distinct neurobiological processes, and these can be better delineated by use of T1-weighted and T2*-weighted MRI measures than cortical thickness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cortical thickness and signal intensity are sensitive for different neurobiological mechanisms, and that signal intensity is a better marker of cortical maturation and aging than thickness.
the cortical thickness measure, which is widely used in the literature, does not provide the full story.
cortical thickness and intracortical signal intensity are sensitive for different neurobiological changes and should therefore not be used interchangeably.
